passage:
I'm Nirmala, and I want to tell you what I learnt on Darshan's staircase. My friend Darshan lost the family shop last month. When I arrived, Darshan was sitting on the third step with a face like stone. My mind raced with things to say: "You'll find something else," "Everything will be okay." All of it felt wrong.
So I sat down two steps below and said nothing. I let the quiet stay. Someone's radio played downstairs. After a long time Darshan's shoulders shook once, and I stayed. We sat together for an hour.
When I finally stood, Darshan said, "Thank you for not saying anything." That was the kindest thing anyone said to me that month.

qa.q: Which step of the staircase was Darshan sitting on?
qa.a: Darshan was sitting on the third step.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling as the comforting phrases ran through the mind?
qa.a: Nirmala felt anxious and unsure, since every phrase seemed wrong. Choosing silence was a way to stay without trying to fix.

qa.q: What did Nirmala choose to do instead of speaking?
qa.a: Nirmala sat down two steps below and let the quiet stay. Being there for an hour showed Darshan's feelings could be borne.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Darshan to have Nirmala sitting silently on the stairs?
qa.a: Darshan probably felt less alone and not pressured to explain or cheer up. Saying "Thank you for not saying anything" shows the silence was a relief.

grounding: A person stays beside a suffering friend without speaking, offering presence only, and does not rush to fill the quiet.

passage:
Community centre coordinator's note, Friday. Outside the hospital ward, Jeevan and Sanjay, friends since college, sat on a plastic bench. Sanjay's father had just been taken in for a long procedure, and there was no news. Sanjay's knee was bouncing.
Several relatives arrived and offered advice and reassurance. Sanjay's face closed more each time. Jeevan simply sat next to Sanjay, handed over a water bottle and said nothing for almost an hour. Once Jeevan touched Sanjay's shoulder.
When the doctor finally came out, Sanjay stood, turned and looked at Jeevan first. Jeevan stood too.
I asked later if Jeevan had wanted to say something. "Yes," Jeevan said, "but Sanjay didn't need words."
Lakshmi, coordinator

qa.q: What did Jeevan hand to Sanjay?
qa.a: Jeevan handed Sanjay a water bottle.

qa.q: What might Jeevan have been feeling while sitting beside Sanjay without speaking?
qa.a: Jeevan may have felt worried and helpless, wanting to say something but choosing to stay. Jeevan said later that Sanjay did not need words.

qa.q: What did Jeevan do that helped Sanjay?
qa.a: Jeevan sat beside Sanjay, handed over water, touched a shoulder once and said nothing for almost an hour. Presence, not advice, was what Jeevan offered.

qa.q: How might Sanjay have felt as relatives kept offering reassurance?
qa.a: Sanjay probably felt more closed in and tired, since Sanjay's face closed each time. Jeevan's silent company was easier to bear.

grounding: A person stays beside a suffering friend outside a hospital ward without speaking, offering presence only, as noted by a coordinator.

passage:
Friday night
Went to Jagdish's flat after work. He didn't get the scholarship he'd worked on for two years. He'd texted just one line: "didn't get it."
When I got there he was sitting on the floor against the sofa, not crying, just still. I wanted to say all the things: there'll be others, their loss, you're brilliant. I had them ready.
I didn't say any of it. I sat on the floor next to him. I made two cups of tea and put one near his hand. We sat for maybe an hour. The ceiling fan clicked. Once he sighed so deeply his shoulders shook, and I just put my hand on his back.
At the end he said, "Thanks for not trying to fix it."
I didn't know silence could say so much.
Mahima

qa.q: What did Jagdish's text say?
qa.a: He'd texted just one line: "didn't get it."

qa.q: Why did Mahima hold back the comforting words ready in mind?
qa.a: Mahima sensed Jagdish was too hurt and stunned for pep talk, and felt that quiet company would comfort him more.

qa.q: What made Mahima's support work?
qa.a: Mahima stayed beside him without filling the quiet, making tea and touching his back, which showed his pain could be borne.

qa.q: How did Jagdish experience the silent hour?
qa.a: Jagdish felt grateful and less alone, thanking Mahima for not trying to fix it.

grounding: A person stays beside a suffering friend without speaking, showing that the friend's feelings can be borne.

passage:
Sangeeta: I failed the final round
Sangeeta: I don't want to talk about it
Jatin: ok
Jatin: can I come sit with you anyway? I won't say anything
Sangeeta: why
Jatin: so you're not alone with it
Sangeeta: ok
[40 min later]
Jatin: outside
[Jatin sat beside her on the steps of her building. Neither of them spoke for a long time. Sangeeta cried once, quietly. Jatin passed her a tissue and looked at the street.]
[later that night]
Sangeeta: thank you for not saying "next time"
Sangeeta: everyone keeps saying next time
Jatin: I'll come tomorrow too, if you want
Sangeeta: yes

qa.q: Where did Jatin sit with Sangeeta?
qa.a: Jatin sat beside her on the steps of her building.

qa.q: Why did Jatin offer to come without talking?
qa.a: Jatin cared about Sangeeta and sensed she was hurting too much for words, and didn't want her to be alone with it.

qa.q: What made Jatin's visit comforting?
qa.a: Jatin stayed beside her in silence, passed a tissue and didn't rush to say "next time", which let her feelings simply be there.

qa.q: What were other people's words like for Sangeeta?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt tired and unheard when everyone kept saying "next time", which is why Jatin's silence felt like relief.

grounding: A person stays beside a suffering friend without speaking, offering presence only, and the friend feels her pain can be borne.

passage:
In the small town, the news came in the morning: the textile unit where Aditi had worked for three years was shutting down. She sat on the ghat by the river all afternoon.
Maria found her there. She had planned to say something useful about other jobs, other towns. Instead, looking at Aditi's face, she simply sat down beside her on the warm stone.
They watched the river. A boat passed. Women washed clothes on the far bank. Aditi's breath caught once, and Maria leaned her shoulder gently against hers.
Neither spoke for nearly an hour.
When the temple bell rang for evening aarti, Aditi said quietly, "You didn't say anything."
"I didn't know what would help."
"That helped."
They walked home together as the lamps came on.

qa.q: Where did Aditi sit all afternoon?
qa.a: She sat on the ghat by the river all afternoon.

qa.q: What was Maria thinking when she saw Aditi's face?
qa.a: Maria felt unsure and sad for Aditi, sensing that useful advice about other jobs would not help in that moment.

qa.q: What made Maria's presence comforting?
qa.a: Maria sat close without speaking and leaned her shoulder against Aditi's, showing that Aditi's grief could be borne without being fixed.

qa.q: How did Aditi experience the hour of silence?
qa.a: Aditi felt comforted and understood, saying Maria's silence was what helped.

grounding: A person stays beside a suffering friend without speaking, offering presence and showing the pain can be borne.

passage: Selin let herself into Ines's flat in Kadıköy with the spare key, the way they had agreed years ago for emergencies. Ines was on the balcony in yesterday's sweater, knees up, staring at the ferries. Five years with Can, over in one phone call the night before. On the tram Selin had rehearsed things to say: he wasn't good enough, you'll be fine, let's go out. She said none of them. She made two glasses of tea, put one by Ines's foot and sat in the other chair. Gulls. A ferry horn. Ines's tea went cold. Once Ines started to speak and stopped; Selin just nodded. After almost an hour, Ines leaned her head on Selin's shoulder and cried properly for the first time. Much later she said, "Thank you for not trying to make it better. I couldn't have taken that."

qa.q: How long had Ines been with Can?
qa.a: Five years.

qa.q: Why did Selin say none of the lines rehearsed on the tram?
qa.a: Selin sensed Ines was too raw for advice or cheering up, and cared more about being with her than fixing anything.

qa.q: What small, kind things did Selin do instead of talking?
qa.a: She made tea, sat nearby, nodded when Ines could not speak, and simply stayed for almost an hour.

qa.q: What did the silent hour mean for Ines?
qa.a: It showed Ines that her sadness could be borne without being rushed, so she finally felt safe enough to cry properly.

grounding: Shows a person staying beside someone in pain without speaking, offering presence only, so the quiet shows her feelings can be borne.
